title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1679: Russia raises its war budget by 27% to a record as it looks to grow its war in 2027
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Exclusives In Ukraine’s Vivaldi offensive, nobody rides in the BTR-60s. Bulgaria’s old troop carriers go into Russian bunkers packed with mines . Too thinly armored for infantry, 110 Bulgarian-donated BTR-60s now go into Russian bunkers near Lyman packed with anti-tank mines and nobody inside. Europe and Ukraine already have the force to stop Russia. What’s missing is the alliance. . The war may reach Europe by 2027; NATO won't be ready until 2035. The fastest deterrent already exists: a declared alliance with Ukraine's combat-proven force. Ukraine’s tanks are fighting from kilometers back. A 1960s Soviet model does that nearly as well . Ukraine captured more than 40 T-62Ms from Russia, mostly during the 2022 counteroffensives, and has not registered a confirmed combat loss since. For years Ukraine could jam or switch off Russia’s battlefield comms. Rassvet may be the first it can’t . Sanctioning the firm behind Russia's Starlink won't stop it. It can make every satellite slower and costlier to build—and the clock is short. Military Russia drained the Kakhovka Reservoir. Now it hides in the dry bed to creep toward Zaporizhzhia . A frontline commander expects small Russian groups to slip into the city by winter. A leading analyst calls that far too categorical—and says the front is moving the other way. Vivaldi counteroffensive advanced after Ukraine took Russia’s drones out of the fight, ISW assesses . Armored vehicles reached heavy Russian fortifications in the Lyman sector without coming under drone attack, which the analysts read as a sign of Ukrainian drone overmatch. Russia’s mass drone attacks on Ukraine have a goal—likely Ukraine’s capitulation by spring 2027, ISW says . Until his new theory of victory has played out, Putin is unlikely to soften his demands or enter serious ceasefire talks, according to ISW. Russia’s pipeline into Kupiansk is now its escape route—with kidnapped civilians as human shields, Ukraine says . Ukrainian drones filmed the column on 27 September. Khartia warned Russia could pass the footage off as an "evacuation" or "rescue" of civilians. Ukraine makes local gains on Pokrovsk front despite sustained Russian attacks . The marines cleared 5 square kilometers and captured two Russian soldiers. A Ukrainian Hornet drone hit a Russian radar 120 km behind the front. It was likely a $100 million Nebo-M . The strike is part of a push to cut Russian logistics and strip Russian forces of radar and electronic warfare systems, a brigade officer says. Ukraine hits railways of Bryansk, Russia’s launchpad for strikes on Kyiv: downed bridge and 28 derailed cars, region’s governor says . Ukraine's drones reportedly hit the region's railways. Intelligence and technology Mavic vs Slavic: Ukrainian developers adapt reconnaissance drones to the modern battlefield . “The drone was developed as a Ukrainian alternative to Chinese commercial quadcopters,” Vyriy Industries said. A Ukrainian firm now rents out drone jammers by the day—but the deposit is the device’s full price . The daily fee comes off a deposit worth the whole device—rent long enough and the jammer becomes yours. Ukraine just caught a Geran-5 at 425 km/h—the jet drone that has often outrun Ukrainian interceptor drones since January . Ukrainian crews now stop just over half of Russia's jet-powered drones, against more than 90% of the older Shaheds, even as Moscow builds them by the thousand. Russia is stepping up fake Ukrainian government pages as bait for recruiting agents, Ukraine’s security service says . Russian intelligence uses the counterfeits to spread disinformation and to harvest data on the Ukrainians who subscribe. Russia is launching a faster Geran-5 at Ukraine that satellite jamming may no longer knock off course, a monitoring channel says . The drone can steer by images of the terrain below, and its extra speed makes it harder for interceptors to catch, though Ukrainian officials have not confirmed the system. International Russia ordered arson attack on Estonian military robot-maker supplying Ukraine, Estonia confirms . Estonia says its intelligence service established that Russia’s special services ordered the August fire at Milrem Robotics, as Russian sabotage operations spreads across Europe. Belgium rushes three F-16s to Ukraine as Russia expands its drone and missile assault . Zelenskyy says the aircraft will arrive by the end of 2026, strengthening Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian air targets and conduct combat missions. Russian jet-powered drone hits near Yahodyn, just 1.5 km from Poland, as Warsaw changes air defense rules . Poland plans to allow decisions to engage aerial targets based on radar data. Lithuania gets its US tank battalion back while the Pentagon weighs pulling up to 40,000 troops from Europe . The Lithuanian leader calls the decision an encouragement and says fewer American soldiers will remain on the continent overall. Humanitarian and social impact Russian troops enter homes and threaten starving Oleshky residents for food and alcohol, officials say . Residents who escaped the occupied Kherson Oblast city describe threats and abuse by Russian troops amid severe shortages of food, water, and medicine. Russian mercenaries blew off African prisoners’ legs to practice battlefield medicine, Wagner fighter says . A Russian mercenary captured by Ukraine describes alleged Wagner training sessions where prisoners were deliberately maimed and killed so recruits could practice battlefield medicine and killing techniques. Russia hits a Kharkiv high-rise overnight, injuring 43 people, then kills four in daylight strikes on central Kyiv and Dnipro . A pre-dawn strike on Ukraine's second city gave way to drone attacks on a business center and then a national science institution during working hours. “Reminiscent of 11 September at World Trade Center”: Russia strikes Ukraine’s century-old National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv, people are climbing onto windows not to be buried alive Political and legal developments Russia raises its war budget by 27% and expands the army again – both to new records – even as its budget deficit widens and oil revenues fall . Moscow plans to spend a record 17.1 trillion rubles on defense in 2027 as it raises taxes and borrowing to cover a widening deficit. The Kremlin calls mobilization talk “nonsense”—Zelenskyy says it has already begun, with North Korean reinforcements . The claim comes from Ukraine's military intelligence, which has tracked Russian preparations for a larger call-up for months. War is costing Ukraine $155 billion per year. With Western aid running late, Kyiv is freezing everything but army, pensions, and public wages . Kyiv froze parks, fountains, and road repairs to pay its army and pensioners first. After Russia hits Kyiv’s Academy of Sciences with jet-powered drone, the Kremlin says Ukraine must “pay a price” . Peskov calls Russia's intensified strikes part of that price. title: Russia’s Jet-Powered Shahed Drones Are Quickly Evolving As Ukraine Scrambles To Blunt Their Damage
body: Over the summer, Russia intensified its use of jet-powered one-way attack drones. Flying faster and higher than the propeller-driven Shahed-136 s (or Geran-2s as Russia calls their copies) that have been terrorizing Ukraine for years, these weapons are far harder to intercept. We predicted this would happen over three years ago when Iran first introduced its jet-powered Shahed-238, which itself was an adaptation of the Shahed-136. Initial variants of Russia’s copy of that drone, called the Geran-3, first appeared over the skies of Ukraine in early 2024 . By mid-2025 they were becoming a real problem . Since then, the latest higher-performance variant of this weapon, the Geran-4, has added great strain to Ukraine’s dwindling air defense resources and is the source of increasing levels of destruction across the country. The Geran-4 appeared last May, according to the Ukrainian Defense Intelligence Directorate (GUR). Unlike the Geran-3, which largely used a modified Shahed-136 airframe, the new drone has one purpose-built for higher-speed flight because “the structural strength [of the older model] was insufficient for high-speed flights, and even less so for maneuvering under high G-loads,” GUR noted. A Geran 4 attempting to be intercepted by a Ukrainian drone. (Via X) (GUR) The Geran-4’s new airframe features a blended air intake and overall “improved aerodynamic efficiency, a reinforced structure, and a turbojet engine with increased thrust,” GUR stated. “The wings are now permanently integrated into the center wing section. To reduce air resistance, the number of technological hatches on the fuselage has been minimized.” In an overnight attack across Ukraine that lasted until Monday, “Russia launched 165 drones overnight, 79 of them jet-powered, the Air Force reported . Air defenses downed or suppressed 112, and hits were recorded at 14 locations.” You can see the aftermath of one of those attacks in the following video. We’re under constant attack Unfortunately, just a few minutes ago, a jet-powered Shahed drone hit a residential building . #Odesa Burn in hell, ruzzians pic.twitter.com/EXTWM1yVIN — Antoninaodesa NAFO (@antoninaodesssa) September 28, 2026 Recently, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL) got its hands on one of these weapons. Its report offers the best view yet of what makes these drones so dangerous. The Geran-4 is “a new, faster version of the attack drone that is proving harder for Ukrainian air defenses to intercept,” the report states. “We were given a rare opportunity to literally take this surviving drone apart and find out what makes it so much faster, more maneuverable, and more accurate.” “The first part we uncover is the turbojet engine. It is one of the Geran-4’s most significant upgrades, allowing the drone to fly at altitudes of up to eight kilometers,” the report explained. “That’s twice as high as the older propeller-powered drones. According to specialists, drones equipped with this type of engine have already flown from Russia-occupied Crimea to Lutsk in northwestern Ukraine, a distance of more than 700 kilometers.” RFE/RL takes apart a Russian Geran-4 drone to uncover what makes the jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) faster, harder to intercept, and capable of operating deep inside Ukraine — from its turbojet engine and advanced camera to foreign-made communications and navigation… pic.twitter.com/WGNdlpS9w1 — Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (@RFERL) September 25, 2026 “This engine allows it to fly at speeds of up to 450 to 500 kilometers per hour over Ukrainian territory. Sometimes even faster,” RFE / RL proffered. “It flies fast and high, which is why it is still difficult to intercept.” As the camera pans down over the engine, the reporters noted that while it is made in China, “we have investigated cases where these engines were assembled in Russia using Chinese components.” The next component examined was the drone’s camera. “It has several modes: daylight, night vision, and infrared,” the report stated. “The camera offers 10-times optical zoom and up to 32-times digital zoom, allowing the drone operator to view terrain from an altitude of eight kilometers.” “If there is a relay station and it is connected to the network, an operator sitting in an automated workstation somewhere in Bryansk, Oryol, or Crimea can control the drone and guide it to its target,” RFE/RL stated. “Once the drone is inside Ukraine, regular cellular SIM cards can help keep it connected,” the report continued. “We also found two GSM modems inside this drone. Using SIM cards, they can transmit the Geran-4’s location over mobile networks, allowing the operator to track it in real time.” Back in 2024, we explained how Shaheds fitted with 4G modems and SIM cards from Ukrainian telecom firms, combined with a camera installed on the drone and the ability to use wireless networks, could be one of a number of avenues that would transform the Shahed into a relatively long-range reconnaissance and strike asset capable of beyond-line-of-sight real-time operations. This could help plug what at the time was a glaring gap in the Russian arsenal, although the stability of its connectivity is still unknown and providing man-in-the-loop guidances in real-time for strikes may be beyond the capabilities of this configuration, at least consistently. Regardless, most of these drones do not have cameras or modems, they fly to a specific set of coordinates and dive on a target before detonating. The following images offered a glimpse into that system. Inside Russian Shahed: power bank and a SIM card of a Ukrainian operator pic.twitter.com/D5LGBMJfIv — MAKS 26 (@Maks_NAFO_FELLA) November 29, 2023 Drone specialists who have investigated the remains of these weapons told the outlet that they had found SIM cards “from Ukraine, Russia, Belarus, and even some European Union countries. And the deeper we go inside the drone, the more foreign-made components we find.” The RFE/RL team also found a Chinese mesh modem the Russians use to help guide the drone. “It’s responsible, among other things, for radio and video communications. Essentially, this device allows the drone operator to see the video feed from the Geran-4 almost in real time,” RFE/RL stated. “The modem has a range of up to 300 kilometers and can also act as a signal relay. That means several drones flying near each other can relay and strengthen the signal, making it possible to control them over much greater distances.” The discovery of the Chinese mesh modem illustrates something we reported earlier this year : “For some time now, Russia has been working on a man-in-the-loop (MITL) control capability for the Shahed/Geran, a feature that was confirmed when they started to appear with cameras and cellular modems, something TWZ explored in detail at the time. These developments allow the drone to be connected to an operator. Standard Shaheds fly autonomous routes to pre-planned targets on autopilot with no man-in-the-loop control. They are ‘fire and forget’ weapons. “ “ Meanwhile, the range at which MITL can be achieved has been steadily increased. At first, the drones were adapted to exploit patchy cellular networks to provide additional connectivity when available. More recently, Shaheds have been flying with antennas allowing for direct line-of-sight control close to the front lines. This allows them to hit targets dynamically like an FPV drone, while packing a much heavier punch and being able to loiter for long periods of time. You can read all about this development here . Now, the datalink range is being extended using airborne signal relays , possibly creating a mesh network with multiple line-of-sight links.” درون”Geran-4“ توقف محرك الـMicro-turbojet قبل الانقضاض على الهدف، وتتَّخذ وضعية الانزلاق البطيء، ربّما لتوفير الوقود او لدقة افضل اثناء البحث بالعدسة البصرية. ايضاً يظهر بوضوح هوائيات الارسال Mesh Antennas اثنان مثبَّتان على الذَّيل، أحدهما موجّه الى الاعلى والاخر الى الاسفل. pic.twitter.com/cQIyHhvbmm — TACTIX (@Tactixtm) September 27, 2026 Finally, the Ukrainian journalists found something else we have long reported on . Like many other Russian weapons, the Geran-4 even contains components made in America. “Despite international sanctions, a significant portion of its components are still coming from abroad, highlighting gaps in global export control enforcement,” RFE/RL showcased. “We just opened up the drone’s onboard computer, and these circuit boards contain components made by a U.S. company. The markings on this component are partly worn off, but you can still see the manufacturer, Texas Instruments.” “According to the specialists, what is actually Russian-made here is mainly the drone’s body and its assembly. This particular drone was manufactured and assembled at Alabuga, a major Russian drone production site . According to Ukraine’s military intelligence, Russia is now producing around 3,000 Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones a month at Alabuga and other facilities across Russia.” Satellite images of the site first emerged in 2023, which you can see below. Satellite images of the factory producing Iranian kamikaze drones Shahed-136 in Yelabuga, Tatarstan. #russia #Ukraine pic.twitter.com/07HBMwcGCs — Dr. Khaled Alfaiomi (@Alfaiomi) November 15, 2023 As if the Geran-4 drones were not challenging enough for Ukraine, Russian Geran-5 jet-powered drones are equipped with “a DSMAC (Digital Sensor Module for Autonomous Navigation) module for navigation using reference images of the Earth’s surface, similar to the X-101 missile,” the Ukrainian technology monitoring channel Polkovnyk GSh reported on Telegram . DSMAC allows for a weapon to navigate without any external help from global positioning satellites. The Tomahawk also uses this system. You can read all about it and how AI embedded in Shahed models will be the next leap in true autonomy far beyond the front lines, even for hunting and killing targets of opportunity, in our special feature linked here. In addition, Russia has installed mesh repeaters on these weapons for radio signals so that video of the attacks can be “recorded (and immediately transmitted),” presidential adviser on defense technology Serhii Beskrestnov, known as Flash, said on Telegram . The Russian military is now capable of acquiring real-time, high-quality BDA of its strikes with Geran-type OWA-UAVs/cruise missiles in downtown Kyiv. In the footage below, we can see the moment of a Russian strike with Geran-5 cruise missile on the "Inkom" business center… pic.twitter.com/mPx4Kf9tmH — Status-6 (@Archer83Able) September 27, 2026 Though these jet-powered drones are causing major problems for Ukraine, the country is finding a way to combat them. One way is by using Ukrainian Air Force F-16 Vipers to shoot them down, which you can see in the following video. The moment a Russian jet-powered "Shahed" drone is shot down by an F-16 fighter jet using its M61 Vulcan cannon. pic.twitter.com/gU72HJTXUa — WarTranslated (@wartranslated) September 23, 2026 The Russian jet-powered drones were largely outrunning the drone interceptors Ukraine began using with great success against the piston-driven Shaheds. Those interceptors were not only saving lives, but they were also saving money because they cost a tiny fraction of far more expensive, higher-end munitions like the PAC-3 MSE fired by the Patriot system or the AIM-120 Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile variants fired from the National Advanced Surface-to-Air Missile System ( NASAMS ) air defense launchers. Seeking a more efficient and effective defense, Ukraine adapted by fielding higher-performing interceptor drones that are purpose-built to take on the jet-powered Russian munitions. Still, the engagement window for hitting the Russian drones is small, and these are more expensive to build. However, they will remain far less costly and faster to acquire than surface-to-air missiles. In his speech earlier this week at the U.N. General Assembly, President Volodymyr Zelensky claimed that “our soldiers have already successfully tested four new jet-powered interceptor drones against Russian jet-powered Shaheds. So we are scaling up production.” It is unclear exactly which interceptors the Ukrainian president was talking about; however, other types designed to take on Russian jet-powered Gerans have become public. One of them is the Sting S, a variant of the bullet-shaped Sting interceptor drone made by the Ukrainian Wild Hornets drone company. On Sept. 19, the company posted a video on X claiming that “a crew from the 1020th Anti-Aircraft Missile Regiment took down a Russian Geran-5 using the new STING S. This drone is faster and carries a larger explosive payload than other Geran variants.” TWZ cannot independently verify these claims. STING S takes down a Geran-5 jet-powered drone-missile The crew from the 1020th Anti-Aircraft Missile Regiment took down a Russian Geran-5 using the new STING S. This drone is faster and carries a larger explosive payload than other Geran variants. Big thanks to the… pic.twitter.com/Eg0rQgd1tL — Wild Hornets (@wilendhornets) September 19, 2026 When we asked for more details, Wild Hornets told us “that the tests are going well. About a dozen enemy ‘Geran-4′ jet-powered strike UAVs have already been shot down, as well as several ‘Geran-5’ models, just in the last few days. We should note that at this stage we are talking about only the first results of combat testing within a few select units.” The Sting S “is a high-speed quadcopter-type interceptor,” the Wild Hornets spokesperson added. “When choosing this model, we took into account that the solution should be inexpensive, easy to use, and quickly scalable.” “Furthermore, most of the targets during combat testing have been destroyed using ‘Hornet Vision Ctrl’ remote control technology,” the spokesman stated. Wild Hornets claims the system provides low-latency image transmission, long-range communication, and resistance to electronic warfare. 100 remote interceptions in 100 seconds: Hornet Vision CTRL in action Since deployment, Ukraine’s Defense Forces have remotely destroyed 1,000+ enemy targets using the system. All thanks to the skill of crews taking down enemy drones with STING interceptors every day pic.twitter.com/9sUthdjsvF — Wild Hornets (@wilendhornets) September 3, 2026 “We expect this will allow us to rapidly scale up the deployment of the new interceptor once mass production begins,” the spokesperson noted. As we have frequently noted , Russia and Ukraine continuously create new weapons and ways to defeat them. The jet-powered Russian drones, and Ukraine’s newest interceptors designed to destroy them, are the latest examples of a seemingly endless weapons evolution cycle in this war. Contact the author: howard@twz.com The post Russia’s Jet-Powered Shahed Drones Are Quickly Evolving As Ukraine Scrambles To Blunt Their Damage appeared first on TWZ .

title: Report Warns of Houthis’ Growing Influence in Horn of Africa
body: Yemen’s Houthi rebels are sending weapons across the Red Sea and sharing technology and knowledge with armed groups in a way that could upend East Africa’s security landscape, a new report shows. The 41-page August 2026 report, “From Spoke to Hub: The Houthis in Africa,” by the nonpartisan think tank Century International details the Houthis’ “multifaceted effort to expand their presence and influence along the African coast of the Gulf of Aden and Red Sea.” “Since the early 2020s, alone and in concert with Iran, the Yemeni group has established itself as a key player in illicit trade in Yemen and its neighborhood; recruited migrants from African countries to serve as smugglers, spies, and soldiers; and built ties not just with al-Shabaab but also with Islamist factions within the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF),” the report states. Interactions with Somalia’s al-Qaida affiliate present a dire threat should the terrorist group obtain advanced Houthi weaponry such as Iranian-style explosives, anti-aircraft missiles and drones. Even more dangerous would be evidence that al-Shabaab had “acquired the knowledge to modify, assemble or eventually manufacture drones locally,” Alex Jalil, a researcher with the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data project (ACLED), told The Africa Report for an August 31 article. The Houthis emerged in the 1990s under the name Ansar Allah, which means “Partisans of God.” They represent the Zaidis, Yemen’s Shia Muslim minority sect, and claim membership in Iran’s “axis of resistance.” The group gained global notoriety by attacking commercial shipping in the Red Sea, a move experts agree is to galvanize domestic support in its chaotic home country. The attacks have wreaked havoc on global shipping and intensified recently as the rebels seized control of Yemen’s port of Mocha and strategic islands near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a vital maritime chokepoint. The Century International report says the Houthis’ expansion strategy resembles that of Lebanon’s Hezbollah terrorist group, also an Iranian proxy. Hezbollah and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), which answers to Iran’s supreme leader and supports militant groups across the Middle East and in Africa, “developed a playbook for building up armed-group capabilities,” the report states. First, terrorists are taught how to wage guerrilla warfare. Then they are taught to use advanced Iranian arms to hit targets up to thousands of kilometers away. “Later, they taught Axis groups to build their own weapons from commercially sourced parts,” the report states. “The evidence is clear: the Houthis with IRGC support have built a network of facilitators across the Red Sea into the Horn of Africa,” Amir Al Bidh, spokesman for Yemen’s Southern Transitional Council (STC), told The National, an Emirati-based news website. “The STC have presented evidence to both the US and UK on the Houthi operational relationship with Al Shabab.” In Sudan, evidence shows that the Houthis have sent operatives to show the SAF how to use and make Iranian drones. In July 2025, the nation’s state-owned Military Industrial Corp. introduced the Safaroog drone, which resembles the Iranian Ababil-T medium-range one-way attack drone. The report indicates that the Sudanese and Iranian drones’ designs are nearly identical. The corporation has close ties to the SAF, which could “significantly alter the course of the civil war” there if it had drone-manufacturing capability, The National reported. If the same drone manufacturing technology and capability were transferred to al-Shabaab, along with a supply of Iranian Saqr anti-aircraft missiles, the security implications for Somalia would be catastrophic. Al-Shabaab and Houthi officials met throughout 2024 in Yemen and Somalia. Among the discussions: al-Shabaab’s procurement of explosive drones. Ahmed Elmi Samatar, an al-Shabaab operative captured in Mukalla, Yemen, in 2024, confessed to being a liaison between the two groups. The Century International report said Samatar “appears to have been coordinating the movement of a group of ‘guests,’ who provided al-Shabaab members with training in improvised explosive device (IED) manufacturing, drone modification, and weapons maintenance.” He also claimed to have set up travel for up to 400 Somalis to “Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen for military and ideological training.” In exchange for weapons and training, the Houthis reportedly want to recruit fighters in Somalia and establish a presence in the country, including setting up communications and surveillance equipment to extend its regional missile and drone capabilities. “At this stage, the evidence seems stronger for training, knowledge transfer and a developing relationship,” ACLED’s Jalil told The Africa Report. “But even if the relationship remains transactional, I think it tells us something important about where Red Sea geopolitics is heading.” Jalil continued: “Transferring knowledge is ultimately much harder to reverse than transferring individual weapons.” The post Report Warns of Houthis’ Growing Influence in Horn of Africa appeared first on Africa Defense Forum .

title: Al-Shabaab Seeks Drones from Houthis
body: Over the last two years, Somalia’s al-Shabaab terrorists have established a relationship with Houthi rebels in Yemen — one that could alter the decades-long battle between the al-Qaida affiliate and government forces in Mogadishu. A new report by The Century Foundation (TCF) public policy research institution outlines the evolving ties between al-Shabaab and the Houthis as the Somalia-based terrorists seek to gain both knowledge and, potentially, technology from the Iranian-backed Houthis. So far, the relationship has been built around training and knowledge transfer, with hundreds of al-Shabaab fighters traveling from their base in southern Somalia to western Yemen to learn drone operation, bomb making and small arms use. Al-Shabaab and the Houthis have nothing in common culturally, linguistically or theologically. Analysts say their relationship is largely transactional: Al-Shabaab wants access to Houthi weaponry, particularly antiaircraft technology; for the Houthis, a footprint on Somali territory could give them greater leverage over shipping through the Gulf of Aden and Bab el-Mandeb Strait while also helping them recruit new fighters. Al-Shabaab fighters have recently died on battlefields in Yemen. “Al-Shabaab is no doubt impressed by the Houthis’ ability to beat back air attacks and launch their own cross-border strikes,” TCF researchers Peter Salisbury, Nadwa Al-Dawsari and Jay Bahadur wrote in their report, based on in-depth interviews, public and private available data, and satellite imagery. “It is difficult to know what concessions the Houthis and al-Shabaab have been able to extract from each other,” they wrote. No current evidence shows that the Houthis have given al-Shabaab access to their own locally manufactured drones and missiles, the researchers noted. “This may reflect a lack of trust between the two groups, or a lack of al-Shabaab absorptive capacity. It may equally be due to a deliberate decision by al-Shabaab to hide new capabilities until it has reason to use them.” “The clearest near-term signal of capability transfer would be the appearance of Iranian-pattern explosive devices, antiaircraft missiles, or drones on Somali battlefields,” the researchers added. Specifically, they wrote, the use of Iranian-developed armor-piercing bombs “would act like a forensic fingerprint of Houthi or Iranian training.” The Houthis have progressed from using off-the-shelf drone technology to manufacturing their own drones and other weapons from imported Iranian parts. They have used that technology to attack commercial ships transiting the Red Sea, Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the Gulf of Aden. The Houthis’ relations with al-Shabaab rests on well-established weapons smuggling routes linking Somalia and Yemen. The TCF report traces al-Shabaab’s relationship with the Houthis to meetings in Yemen in March 2024 followed by Houthi visits to al-Shabaab territory in June and July. In August 2024, authorities in Somalia’s Puntland region confiscated five kamikaze-style drones that were in transit from the Houthis to al-Shabaab. Those drones were based on commercial off-the-shelf technology, unlike the Houthis’ more recent drones built from imported parts. Al-Shabaab acquiring Houthi-built drones would be a significant escalation in al-Shabaab’s relationship with the Houthis as well as its capacity for harm, according to TCF researchers. “Any documented shift in al-Shabaab’s drone use — a shift from the commercial off-the-shelf platforms it currently employs for basic reconnaissance toward purpose-built one-way attack drones of the kind the Houthis manufacture — would also indicate that the relationship has moved from training to active capability transfer,” they added. The post Al-Shabaab Seeks Drones from Houthis appeared first on Africa Defense Forum .

title: Belgium rushes three F-16s to Ukraine as Russia expands its drone and missile assault
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Ukraine is set to receive three more F-16 fighter jets from Belgium by the end of 2026, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, as Russia intensifies its missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian cities. The aircraft are particularly valuable as Russia increases its use of Shahed/Geran drones, including faster jet-powered variants that are harder for Ukraine’s cheaper interceptor drones to stop. Russia’s growing aerial campaign is already placing additional pressure on Ukraine’s limited air-defense resources. Zelenskyy said the aircraft will be delivered through an accelerated process. Ukraine has already received urgent F-16 ammunition from Belgium and other partners, including Spain. “As Russia escalates its attacks every day, we need to increase our capabilities to shoot down aerial targets and protect people,” Zelenskyy said. F-16s help counter Russia’s air campaign Ukraine received its first F-16s in 20 2 4 after an 18-month international effort to secure the aircraft and train Ukrainian pilots. The jets have since become an important part of Ukraine’s air defense. Ukrainian F-16s are used primarily to intercept Russian cruise missiles and attack drones, while also carrying out electronic warfare and other missions. In one January 2025 mission , a Ukrainian F-16 pilot shot down six Russian cruise missiles. Explore further Allies supplied the F-16s — Ukrainian pilots figured out the tactics F-16s can also carry precision-guided bombs and air-to-air missiles, allowing them to support strikes against Russian forces and other targets near the frontline. Ukrainian pilots have developed tactics for using the aircraft despite Russia’s dense air-defense network. For Ukraine, the additional jets therefore provide both another layer against Russia’s expanding aerial attacks and additional capacity for combat operations on the frontline. title: Russian mercenaries blew off African prisoners’ legs to practice battlefield medicine, Wagner fighter says
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); A former Wagner fighter captured by Ukraine has described alleged training sessions in Mali where Russian mercenaries used African prisoners as live subjects, deliberately inflicting severe injuries so recruits could practice battlefield medicine and killing. Training built around real victims The fighter told Ukrainian journalist Dmytro Karpenko that Wagner instructors brought captured Africans to training sessions and turned them into human practice targets. “We gathered for medical training, and they brought in a captured terrorist. They tied a block of TNT to his leg. They set it off, everyone moved away, and of course his leg was blown off,” he said. The recruits then practiced stopping the resulting bleeding. According to the fighter, the prisoner was later shot in the artery near his armpit so they could practice the same procedure on his arm. The prisoner died after the training. In another session, he said, instructors had a prisoner's leg chopped off with an ax so recruits could practice applying a tourniquet under realistic conditions. “They cut off his leg. Then they put on the tourniquet – everything as if it were an extreme situation, so everything would be realistic,” he said. ‘Here, strike the heart’ The alleged exercises also included training in how to kill. The fighter said another prisoner was drugged before recruits were taught how to kill someone with a knife. “They showed us how to kill with a knife to the heart. They chose two people who were willing and said: ‘Here, strike the heart,’” he said. The fighter said all three prisoners died during the exercises. A former Wagner fighter captured by Ukraine, who described alleged abuses committed by Russian mercenaries in Mali in interview with Ukrainian journalist Dmytro Karpenko. Screenshot from video: Dmytro Karpenko From Mali to Ukraine The testimony comes from a Russian mercenary who joined Wagner in 2023 and was sent to Mali that September via Syria. He said around 120–130 recruits traveled with him and that Wagner paid them $3,000 a month. Wagner was a Russian paramilitary formation that operated as a deniable arm of the Kremlin in Ukraine, Syria, and Africa. After Wagner chief Yevgeny Prigozhin's death in 2023, the group's independent role was largely dismantled, with many of its fighters and operations brought under Russian state control. Its African operations were increasingly taken over by Russia's state-run Africa Corps. The mercenary remained in Mali until April 2024. After returning to Russia, he signed a contract with the Russian Defense Ministry in August 2025 and was assigned to the 14th Separate Special Forces Brigade, which is subordinate to Russia's military intelligence agency, the GRU. He was subsequently captured by Ukrainian forces. A record of alleged abuses The account has not been independently verified, but it adds to years of allegations of serious abuses by Wagner and other Russian personnel in Africa. Wagner fighters have long faced allegations of abuses in Africa, including killings and violence against civilians. In Mali, the group became a key part of Russia’s military presence after the country’s military junta turned to Moscow for support, with Wagner fighters operating alongside Malian forces. Ukrainian intelligence has also documented and targeted Wagner’s activities in Africa. The pattern of alleged abuses has continued under Russia’s Africa Corps, the Kremlin-controlled force that replaced Wagner in Mali. Human Rights Watch reported in August 2026 that Africa Corps fighters summarily killed nine civilians , including four children, beat dozens of others, and burned and looted homes in central Mali. In June, the group also carried out airstrikes that killed eight civilians, including three children. Read also The EU sanctioned Russia’s Starlink rival but not the company that builds it. title: Russia drained the Kakhovka Reservoir. Now it hides in the dry bed to creep toward Zaporizhzhia
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Small groups of Russian infantry could slip into regional capital Zaporizhzhia this winter, a frontline commander warned in a mid-September interview with Dnipro TV, in a debate later compiled by Radio Svoboda . His forecast drew quick pushback from a military analyst, who called it far more categorical than the situation warrants. At the center of the dispute lies the drained Kakhovka Reservoir, whose dry bed Russia now uses for cover . Dense drone surveillance has made large mechanized assaults costly, pushing Russian commanders toward small groups that probe for gaps . That shift turns unwatched terrain — here, the drained reservoir bed—into the seams they test. Solitary groups, not massed forces Dmytro Filatov, callsign Perun, commands the 1st Separate Assault Regiment named after Dmytro Kotsiubailo. The danger will come not as a massed assault but as infiltration, he said . He expects solitary infantry groups to reach and enter Zaporizhzhia over the winter. He pointed to the Stepnohirsk axis and the dense buildings along the Dnipro shore. Fog and rain raise pressure across the whole front, and Russian troops have long fought well in winter, he said. A city on the front's edge Zaporizhzhia is a regional capital and industrial center in southeastern Ukraine, with more than 700,000 residents before the full-scale invasion. The city sits about 25 km from the nearest active front, around Stepnohirsk to the south—unusually close for a regional capital of its size. Russian missiles, drones, and glide bombs hit the city daily. It has held since 2022, and Russia has not taken a Ukrainian regional capital since the war's first months. The aftermath of the Russian attack on Zaporizhzhia on 30 May 2026. Credit: Local Governor Ivan Fedorov The dead reservoir as cover Russia blew up the Kakhovka dam in June 2023 and drained the reservoir behind it. Reeds now stand several meters high across the dry basin, giving foot soldiers cover to move unseen. Ukraine's Southern Defense Forces reported in November 2025 that Russian groups use it to press into the Ukrainian flank. Russian troops increasingly use the bed to infiltrate and haul supplies, said Kostiantyn Mashovets of the Information Resistance group. One of their assault groups pushed as far as Malokaterynivka before Ukrainian forces blocked it, he wrote . Ukrainian troops hold northern Plavni, including the railway station and part of the E-105 highway, Mashovets added. The Institute for the Study of War pointed to the same route in its 26 September assessment , citing Ukrainian military observers. Explore further “The worst environmental catastrophe since Chornobyl disaster”: Three years after Russia destroyed Kakhovka Dam, real death toll is still unknown An analyst is not convinced Oleksandr Kovalenko, a military-political expert and Information Resistance coordinator, rates the threat far lower. He wrote that the warning "sounded far more categorical than it should have." Stepnohirsk, about 25 km south of Zaporizhzhia, is the closest active fighting to the city. Russia has tried for years to take the town but now controls only its 3rd microdistrict and southern Plavni. Infiltration becomes possible only if Russia takes the whole foothold and reaches the north bank of the Konka river. That will not happen by the end of 2026, and no ground push on the city looks possible, he said. The main danger stays daily Russian strikes on the city, not a ground advance, he added.
